units.title: Module 1: Development of practical skills in biology

topics.title: 1.1 Practical skills assessed in a written examination

outcomes.text: Design experiments to solve problems in a practical context, choosing suitable apparatus, equipment and techniques.
Identify the variables that must be controlled.
Evaluate whether an experimental method is appropriate for the expected outcomes.
Use a wide range of practical apparatus and techniques correctly.
Use appropriate units for measurements.
Present observations and data in an appropriate format.
Process, analyse and interpret qualitative and quantitative results, reaching valid conclusions.
Use appropriate mathematical skills to analyse quantitative data.
Use significant figures appropriately.
Plot and interpret graphs with labelled axes, scales and units, and measure gradients and intercepts.
Evaluate results and draw conclusions.
Identify anomalies in experimental measurements.
Describe limitations in experimental procedures.
Assess precision and accuracy, including margins of error, percentage errors and apparatus uncertainties.
Refine experimental design by suggesting improvements to procedures and apparatus.

units.title: Module 2: Cells, chemicals for life, transport and gas exchange

outcomes.text: Explain the importance of microscopy in developing cell theory and investigating cell structure, and describe how blood smears are prepared for light microscopy.
Describe differential staining, such as Leishman's stain to identify leucocytes.
Describe animal cell structure using blood cells seen under the light microscope, and observe, draw and annotate them.
Use linear dimensions of cells and the magnification formula.
Use a haemocytometer to count cells, including dilutions and concentration calculations.
Explain the principles and use of flow cytometry in blood analysis.
Describe the ultrastructure and functions of organelles of a typical eukaryotic animal cell seen by electron microscopy.
Describe the ultrastructure of a eukaryotic plant cell and a prokaryotic cell, and compare plant, animal and prokaryotic cells.
Use a graticule and stage micrometer to measure cell dimensions and calculate magnification.
Explain how the plasma membrane is built from modified lipids and how triglycerides and phospholipids relate structure to function.
Describe the fluid mosaic model of the plasma membrane.
Describe diffusion, facilitated diffusion, active transport, endocytosis and exocytosis across membranes.
Investigate factors affecting diffusion rates in cells.
Describe the roles of membranes within and at the surface of cells.
Explain how organelles work together in producing and secreting proteins.
Describe the properties of water, including polarity, hydrogen bonding and its role as a solvent.
Explain the importance of water as a constituent of cell and body fluids and as a transport medium in plants and animals, and analyse data on body fluid composition.
Describe how sugars and proteins in body fluids and plant extracts are detected and measured, including the Biuret test, Benedict's test and colorimetry.
Explain hydrolysis and condensation of biological molecules, and the idea of monomers and polymers.
Describe the ring structure of alpha-glucose as a monosaccharide and lactose as a disaccharide.
Explain how polysaccharides form by condensation with 1,4 and 1,6 glycosidic bonds, and how branching affects solubility; test for starch.
Explain osmosis as movement of water down a water potential gradient, including effects of solutes on cells.
Investigate factors affecting osmosis in plant and animal cells.
Describe the basic structure of an amino acid and peptide bond formation, and use chromatography with Rf values to identify amino acids.
Describe the structure of globular proteins, as shown by enzymes and haemoglobin.
Explain how globular protein structure lets enzymes catalyse specific reactions.
Describe and investigate factors affecting the rate of enzyme-catalysed reactions.
Describe the role of proteins in blood clotting as an enzyme-controlled process, and first-aid to assist clotting.
Describe the use of enzymes and inhibitors in medical diagnosis and treatment.
Describe blood donation, blood groups, and the collection and use of whole blood, leuco-depleted blood, packed red cells, platelets, clotting factors and plasma.
Describe the nucleotide as the monomer of nucleic acids, RNA versus DNA nucleotides, and phosphodiester bonds.
Describe the structure of ADP and ATP as phosphorylated nucleotides.
Describe DNA structure, including evidence for complementary base pairing, and purify DNA by precipitation.
Explain semi-conservative DNA replication, including helicase, DNA polymerase and random mutations.
Describe the genetic code as triplet, non-overlapping, degenerate and universal, and how a gene sets amino acid order.
Describe RNA structure and how it differs from DNA.
Describe transcription and translation of genes to make polypeptides, with mRNA, tRNA, rRNA and RNA polymerase.
Explain the need for a mass transport system in mammals, using surface area to volume ratio.
Describe the internal and external structure of the mammalian heart, including dissection.
Describe the cardiac cycle, including valves and pressure changes.
Explain how heart action is initiated and coordinated by the SAN, AVN and purkyne tissue.
Investigate factors affecting heart rate, including exercise.
Calculate cardiac output from heart rate and stroke volume.
Measure and interpret pulse rate using primary and secondary data.
Interpret an ECG, including tachycardia, bradycardia, S-T elevation and fibrillation.
Describe emergency treatment for a heart attack and cardiac arrest, including defibrillator use.
Explain the importance of a closed double circulatory system.
Describe the structure and functions of arteries, arterioles, capillaries, venules and veins, including sections under the light microscope.
Explain the formation and importance of tissue fluid, with hydrostatic and oncotic pressure.
Measure systolic and diastolic blood pressure with a sphygmomanometer and compare readings.
Interpret blood pressure measurements, including hypertension and hypotension and their consequences.
Relate cells, tissues and organs of the mammalian gas exchange system and observe them with a microscope.
Explain gas exchange in the alveoli, including ventilation, epithelium, surfactant and concentration gradients.
Describe parameters of pulmonary ventilation: tidal volume, breathing rate, vital capacity, residual volume, PEFR and FEV1.
Describe how expired air resuscitation is carried out on adults, children and babies.
Describe gas exchange in terrestrial plants through stomata and lenticels.
Describe the structure of stomata and how they open and close through guard cell turgor and ATP.
Describe the microscopic appearance of stomata in different terrestrial plants.
Explain the need for transport systems in multicellular plants.
Describe the structure, function and location of xylem, phloem and companion cells in roots, stems and leaves of cereals and broad-leaved crops.
Observe, draw and dissect plant tissues to show the position and structure of vascular tissue.

subtopics.title: Water and sugar transport in plants

outcomes.text: Explain entry and transport of water in plants, including adhesion, cohesion and the transpiration stream in terms of water potential.
Explain transpiration, the factors affecting its rate, and investigate it.
Explain translocation as an energy-requiring process between sources and sinks, including active loading and removal.

units.title: Module 3: Cell division, development and disease control

outcomes.text: Describe the cell cycle: interphase (G1, S, G2), mitosis and cytokinesis giving identical daughter cells.
Describe the changes in nuclei and cells during mitosis in animals and plants, and recognise stages under the microscope.
Describe the stages and features of apoptosis.
Explain the importance of apoptosis and mitosis in growth and repair.
Explain differentiation of stem cells into specialised cells, including totipotent, pluripotent and multipotent cells.
Describe current applications and uses of stem cells, including bone marrow stem cells.
Explain the significance of meiosis in sexual reproduction and producing haploid gametes.
Describe the stages of meiosis in plant and animal cells.
Explain how meiosis produces genetically different daughter cells through crossing over and independent assortment.
Describe the programme of antenatal care in the United Kingdom.
Describe dietary changes recommended in pregnancy and why nutrient recommendations change.
Describe the effects of alcohol and smoking on fetal growth and development.
Use ultrasound measurements and fetal growth charts to assess fetal growth.
Evaluate techniques for assessing fetal development and detecting disorders: ultrasonography, amniocentesis and chorionic villus sampling.
Describe the production and use of karyotypes, including for Down's, Klinefelter's and Turner's syndromes.
Describe biological classification, taxonomic ranks and the biological and phylogenetic species concepts.
Describe the types of evidence used in classification and how theories change with new evidence.
Describe the use of DNA barcoding and the genes used.
Interpret phylogenetic trees and genetic data to show relatedness.
Describe behavioural, physiological and anatomical adaptations in Homo sapiens and plant adaptations to extremes of temperature, light and water, with a practical investigation.
Discuss the evolution of language as a scientific question with competing theories.
Explain adaptation and selection as components of evolution.
Define and measure biodiversity, including Simpson's Index of Diversity, at genetic, species and ecosystem levels.
Calculate genetic diversity within populations from the proportion of polymorphic gene loci.
Explain how bacteria, viruses and fungi cause communicable disease.
Describe the causes, transmission, symptoms and treatment of tuberculosis and HIV/AIDS.
Describe the structure of HIV.
Identify bacteria using Gram staining and cell and colony morphology, and culture bacteria.
Explain how the incidence and prevalence of a communicable disease change over time, including endemic, epidemic and pandemic.
Calculate incidence, prevalence and mortality rates and explain their importance.
Analyse and interpret epidemiological data.
Explain the importance of reporting notifiable diseases and the role of Public Health England.
Discuss social, ethical, economic and biological factors in controlling HIV/AIDS and TB.
Describe primary and non-specific defences, including phagocytosis and inflammation.
Describe how phagocytes act.
Describe the roles of B and T lymphocytes in the specific immune response.
Explain the secondary immune response and memory cells in long term immunity.
Describe antibody structure and function, including opsonins and agglutinins.
Describe how people are tested for TB and HIV infection.
Distinguish active from passive immunity and natural from artificial immunity.
Explain how allergies arise from immune hypersensitivity.
Explain the principles of vaccination, forms of vaccines and booster vaccinations.
Explain the role of vaccination programmes in preventing epidemics, including herd immunity.
Describe biological and practical problems in developing and using vaccines.
Discuss the ethical issues in developing and using vaccines, such as the HPV vaccine.
Describe how antibiotics are used in treating communicable disease and why they act on bacterial but not human cells.
Explain how antibiotic misuse leads to resistant strains of bacteria.
Investigate the effect of antibiotics on Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria.
Identify risk factors for non-communicable diseases such as cancers and asthma, and evaluate epidemiological evidence of correlation.
Describe the cellular basis of cancer, including cell cycle control and tumour and metastasis formation.
Explain how mutations of proto-oncogenes (Ras, Myc) lead to cancer.
Explain how mutations of tumour suppressor genes such as p53 lead to cancer.
Evaluate epidemiological evidence linking risk factors to cancers, such as smoking, diet and BRCA1.
Describe methods used to detect cancers, such as MRI, X-rays, CT, PET, ultrasound, biopsies and blood tests.
Discuss ethical and economic issues in cancer screening and genetic testing.
Describe cancer treatments: surgery, chemotherapy, radiotherapy, immunotherapy, complementary and hormone-related treatments.
Describe short- and long-term effects of pollutants on the respiratory system, such as tobacco smoke, asbestos and fungal spores.
Describe causes and symptoms of chronic bronchitis, emphysema, asthma and lung cancer.
Compare acute and chronic diseases.
Describe the treatment of asthma with beta agonists and steroids.
Explain the importance of plants as sources of medicinal drugs.
Describe the design and use of clinical trials, including phases, sample size, randomisation, placebos and double-blind trials.
Describe the role of NICE in providing treatment guidelines and the importance of economic considerations.
Outline glycolysis as an enzyme-controlled pathway.
Outline the link reaction.
Outline the Krebs cycle.
Outline oxidative phosphorylation, including electron carriers, proton gradients and ATP synthase.
Outline anaerobic respiration in muscle cells and yeast.
Calculate and interpret respiratory quotients to compare energy values of respiratory substrates.
Investigate the rate of respiration with respirometers and the effects of temperature, substrate, anaerobic conditions and different substrates.
Describe immediate and long-term effects of exercise on the respiratory and cardiovascular systems and skeletal muscle.
Describe factors affecting aerobic fitness.
Investigate factors affecting resting heart rate, breathing rate or recovery times.
Explain how training improves aerobic fitness using the F.I.T.T. factors.
Evaluate supplementary methods of enhancing performance: carbohydrate loading, RhEPO, blood doping and steroids.
Explain the significance of VO2 max as a measure of aerobic fitness.
Describe the role of haemoglobin in oxygen transport.
Compare oxygen dissociation curves for adult haemoglobin, fetal haemoglobin and myoglobin.
Explain the factors affecting oxygen dissociation, including carbonic anhydrase.
Explain oxygen deficit and oxygen debt (EPOC).
Describe the histology and ultrastructure of skeletal muscle, with microscopy and muscle dissection.
Explain the sliding filament theory of muscle contraction, including actin, myosin, troponin, tropomyosin, ATP and calcium ions.
Identify the parts of the male and female urinogenital systems.
Describe the histology of the ovaries and testes.
Describe gametogenesis (oogenesis and spermatogenesis) and relate it to mitosis and meiosis.
Relate the structure of the secondary oocyte and sperm to function.
Explain the role of hormones in gametogenesis and the menstrual cycle.
Describe fertilisation and its importance in restoring chromosome number and adding variation.
Describe the use of monoclonal antibodies in pregnancy testing.
Evaluate biological and ethical issues around infertility.
Describe assisted reproduction techniques such as IUI, IVF and ICSI.
Describe the effects of ageing on the female reproductive system, including menopause.
Describe management of these effects, including HRT and its advantages and disadvantages.
Describe the effects of ageing on the male urinogenital system, including benign prostate hyperplasia.
Describe chloroplast ultrastructure and where the light-dependent and light-independent reactions occur, and separate pigments by chromatography.
Describe the light-dependent stage, transferring light energy to ATP and reduced NADP.
Describe the light-independent stage (Calvin cycle), including CO2, RuBisCO, RuBP, GP and TP.
Investigate factors affecting photosynthesis and the Hill reaction with DCPIP.
Explain how TP and GP are used to make carbohydrates, lipids and amino acids.
Explain the dependence of respiration in plants and animals on photosynthesis products.
Explain the biological significance of the compensation point for crop production and compare it between leaf samples.
Explain the importance of microorganisms in the nitrogen cycle and as biosensors in environmental monitoring.
Culture Rhizobium and investigate root nodules in legumes.
Describe the transfer of biomass through a food chain in food production.
Evaluate the efficiency of biomass transfer and sustainability of resource provision, for example fish farming versus beef.
Describe the role of ruminants and their gut microorganisms in the human food chain.
Describe farms as ecosystems and the conflict between agriculture and conservation, comparing intensive and extensive farming.
Explain how land management, such as forestry and agriculture, can deflect succession.
Investigate differences in biodiversity using random and systematic sampling.
Explain factors altering birth and death rates in human populations and interpret demographic charts.
Describe the impact of rising human population on ecosystems and biodiversity.
Explain the ecological, economic and scientific importance of species biodiversity and statistical methods to assess it.
Discuss the global food security agenda, sustainable food production and the role of the UN Food and Agriculture Organisation.
Explain the control of flowering, including vernalisation and phytochrome.
Describe adaptations of flowers for wind and insect pollination.
Describe fertilisation and seed formation, including the pollen tube, embryo and endosperm.
Describe seed germination, factors affecting it, and the role of gibberellin.
Explain the importance of cereals as staple foods and the food security and sustainability issues involved.

topics.title: 5.1 Genetics in the twenty first century

outcomes.text: Explain monogenic inheritance using gene, allele, locus, genotype, phenotype, dominant, recessive and codominant correctly.
Describe gene mutations, such as cystic fibrosis, sickle cell anaemia, PKU and Huntington's disease.
Describe codominance and multiple alleles, as in blood groups and HLA antigens.
Describe sex linkage and autosomal linkage.
Use model organisms such as Drosophila, dihybrid inheritance and the chi-squared test to analyse inheritance patterns.
Describe chromosome mutations in humans, including non-disjunction and translocation.
Explain the role of the genetic counsellor, pedigree analysis, genetic testing and the ethical issues.
Explain how natural selection changes allele frequencies, using malaria and the sickle cell allele.
Link changes in amino acid sequence to changes in protein structure and properties.
Use the Hardy-Weinberg equations to analyse changes in allele frequencies.
Explain how the founder effect and genetic bottlenecks contribute to genetic differences between populations.
Explain the role of geographical and reproductive isolation in forming new species.
Explain epigenetics and the effect of environment on gene expression, including DNA methylation, histones and human epigenetic studies.
Explain post-transcriptional editing of mRNA, introns and exons.
Describe genetic modification of bacteria to make human proteins such as insulin, using restriction enzymes, ligase, plasmids and reporter genes.
Explain the principles and uses of PCR, including primers, Taq polymerase and log scales.
Explain the principles and uses of agarose gel electrophoresis.
Describe the use of haplotypes, SNPs and VNTRs in human genome studies.
Outline genetic engineering of eukaryotic cells: knockout mice, human proteins in animals and genetically modified crops.
Distinguish somatic from germ line gene therapy and discuss the ethics.
Outline the principles of RNA interference using siRNA and miRNA.
Describe the organisation of the somatic and autonomic nervous system and observe nervous tissue.
Describe the structure and function of the human brain regions.
Describe the structure of motor, sensory and relay neurones.
Explain the resting potential and transmission of the action potential in neurones.
Describe synapse structure and function, including neurotransmitters and excitatory and inhibitory potentials.
Describe the reflex arc and reflexes used to assess nervous damage, and investigate reflexes and reaction times.
Describe the use of brain scans to assess brain and spinal cord damage.
Describe consequences of brain and spinal cord damage and the ethics of establishing brain death.
Describe the use of drugs to modify brain activity and the effects of heroin, cannabis, methamphetamine and alcohol on synapses.
Describe psychological and physical drug dependency and its consequences.
Describe the structure of the eye and the function of each part.
Describe the structure of the retina, including rods, cones, bipolar and ganglion cells, fovea and blind spot.
Explain the retina as a receptor of light and a transducer.
Describe routine eye tests, including visual acuity, colour vision and OCT scans.
Describe the symptoms and possible causes of Alzheimer's disease.
Describe the effects of ageing on the nervous system, including hearing and visual impairment and memory loss.
Investigate the effect of ageing on reaction times and memory.
Explain homeostasis, receptors, effectors, negative feedback, normal ranges and positive feedback with oxytocin.
Explain nervous and hormonal control of heart rate.
Explain the control of body temperature and the responses to rising and falling temperature.
Explain regulation of thyroxine release and its effect on metabolic rate.
Describe how core body temperature is measured and why it matters.
Describe the causes, symptoms and treatment of hypothermia and hyperthermia.
Describe the pancreas as an endocrine gland, including the Islets of Langerhans.
Explain regulation of blood glucose by negative feedback, with insulin and glucagon.
Describe the types of diabetes, their causes, risk factors and diagnosis.
Describe the fasting blood glucose test, glucose tolerance testing and biosensors.
Describe treatment and management of Type 1 and Type 2 diabetes.
Describe the team of health professionals who manage diabetes and evidence-based practice.
Discuss the future impact of diabetes on the human population.
Explain why excretory products are removed, including deamination and urea production.
Describe the gross structure of the kidney and associated organs.
Describe the nephron and how ultrafiltration and selective reabsorption produce urine.
Explain the role of the kidney in osmoregulation, including ADH and aquaporins.
Describe the kidney as an endocrine gland, including EPO and renin.
Describe causes, diagnosis and consequences of kidney failure.
Compare haemodialysis and peritoneal dialysis.
Discuss kidney transplants, therapeutic and reproductive cloning, and stem cell technology.
